table.ruleA: Add the charge-table amount for this cycle to each form; volume not enforced.
table.ruleB: Add the inflow-schedule amount for this cycle to each tank; volume not enforced.

table.ruleA: Forms 1 to 6 in order, one at a time; if contents > volume, excess goes to form n+1 before it is handled (cascades); form 6 excess goes to waste tally; contents = volume does nothing.
table.ruleB: Tanks 1 to 6 in order, one at a time; if contents > volume, excess goes to tank n+1 before it is handled (cascades); tank 6 excess goes to outfall total; equal to volume does nothing.

table.ruleA: Read contents after Step 2. GREEN and >= upper mark becomes HOT; HOT and <= lower mark becomes GREEN; otherwise unchanged; at most one change per cycle; logged as (cycle, form, before, after).
table.ruleB: Read contents after Step 2. STEADY and >= upper mark becomes OVERLOADED; OVERLOADED and <= lower mark becomes STEADY; otherwise unchanged; at most one change per cycle; logged as (cycle, tank, before, after).

table.ruleA: Compute all six amounts first from contents at start of step (GREEN: floor of quarter; HOT: floor of half), then apply together: each loses its amount; GREEN amount to waste; HOT amount to form n-1; HOT form 1 to waste. Volume not enforced.
table.ruleB: Tanks 1 to 6 sequentially, amount from contents when reached (STEADY: floor of quarter; OVERLOADED: floor of half), applied immediately: loses amount; STEADY amount to outfall; OVERLOADED amount to tank n-1; OVERLOADED tank 1 to outfall. Volume not enforced.
table.difference: The wording differs (simultaneous vs sequential), but the function does not. Transfers only go upstream (n to n-1). In B's 1-to-6 order, tank n-1 has already been handled by the time it receives tank n's return, and nothing reaches tank n before it is handled (only tank n+1 sends to it, and n+1 comes later). So every tank's amount is computed from its start-of-step contents, exactly as in A. Rounding applies to each position's own contents in both.

table.ruleA: Sum all six forms; if total > 38 (strictly), every form becomes floor(half); all removed units go to waste; record the cycle. Total of 38 or less: nothing.
table.ruleB: Sum all six tanks; if total > 38 (strictly), every tank becomes floor(half); all removed liquor goes to outfall; log the cycle. Total of 38 or less: nothing.

table.ruleA: After cycle 5 Step 5: (a) end mix by form, (b) end status, (c) all status changes, (d) washout cycles, (e) waste tally, (f) balance check.
table.ruleB: After cycle 5 Step 5: (a) end contents by tank, (b) end state, (c) all state changes, (d) bypass cycles, (e) outfall total, (f) balance check, showing both sides.
table.difference: B asks for both sides of the balance check to be shown. That is presentation only.

result.probeWhy: The only suspected difference was Step 4: simultaneous in A, sequential in B. The probe starts every position at or near its volume and adds heavy inflow, so in cycle 1 all six positions go HOT/OVERLOADED, including position 1, which sends its return to the loss tally. That puts adjacent HOT pairs in Step 4 in five cycles, so returned amounts land on neighbours in both directions of handling order. A zero row, an all-9 row and alternating rows push the total above 38 in several cycles (washouts in cycles 1, 3 and 4) and also produce HOT-to-GREEN reversals. The printed tables separately trip the equality edge: the Step 5 total is exactly 38 in one cycle and no halving fires in either document. I also compared the two over 200,000 random start/input sets with a script and found 0 differences.
result.differingRule: None. The only wording difference is in Step 4: A computes every amount first and applies them together, while B handles the tanks one at a time from 1 to 6. This gives the same result because each return goes only to the previous tank, which B has already handled.
result.trust: Both routes agree. The table argument is a proof for all inputs, not just a sample.
